layers: Planet spheres (Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter)

hotspots.label: Mercury's slow spin
hotspots.description: Mercury rotates so slowly that one day lasts about 176 Earth days — longer than its 88-day year.
hotspots.positionHint: Leftmost sphere in the row. Smallest of the five (radius ~0.24), muted grey-ochre with crater mottling, its pointer dot barely creeping.
hotspots.function: Demonstrates the slowest spinner of the row.

hotspots.label: Venus's backward spin
hotspots.description: Venus rotates in the opposite direction to most planets (retrograde) — on Venus the Sun rises in the west — and one day lasts about 117 Earth days.
hotspots.positionHint: Second sphere from the left (radius ~0.4), warm cream surface. A small retrograde arrow label shows its reversed spin relative to the other four.
hotspots.function: Shows retrograde rotation and the longest day measured by the row's counter.

hotspots.label: Earth's 24-hour day
hotspots.description: Earth rotates once every 24 hours. The pointer dot on its surface makes one complete circle and the day counter ticks 24:00.
hotspots.positionHint: Center sphere (radius ~0.42), dusty blue-green mottling. The reference spinner whose counter anchors the lesson.
hotspots.function: The reference rotation — every other planet's day is compared to this one.

hotspots.label: Mars's near-twin spin
hotspots.description: Mars rotates almost as fast as Earth — about 24.6 hours per day — despite being more than half Earth's size.
hotspots.positionHint: Fourth sphere in the row, muted rust mottling. Its counter nearly matches Earth's.

hotspots.label: Jupiter's lightning spin
hotspots.description: The biggest planet spins the fastest — one rotation in about 9.9 hours. Its day counter races past two Earth days every 24 hours.
hotspots.positionHint: Rightmost sphere in the row (radius ~0.62), cream-and-tan banded. Its counter ticks the fastest of all five.

hotspots.label: Retrograde marker
hotspots.description: A small direction arrow showing that Venus's rotation runs the opposite way from the other four planets.
hotspots.positionHint: Floating above the Venus sphere, a half-ring arrow pointing the reverse direction from the Mars/Earth/Jupiter arrows.

hotspots.label: Rotation axis
hotspots.description: The invisible rod each sphere spins around — the axis of rotation. Every planet rotates around its own axis.
hotspots.positionHint: Floating near Earth's top pole with a short dashed line down through the sphere's center.

visualStyleNotes: Anatomy Atelier quality bar throughout: warm off-white studio backdrop, no floor grid, no glow, no bloom, no emissive materials, no cartoon outlines. Five planet spheres float in a row on a soft radial ground-shadow. Each sphere carries one small warm-grey pointer-dot on its surface and a slim floating day counter beneath (text panel). Spin motion is real-time at accelerated scale per planet, synchronized to Earth's 24h mark. The axis overlay and Venus retrograde arrow are thin, matte, low-key line geometry in branch colors, appearing via layer toggle. The pointer dots and hotspot dots are the only saturated accents.
materialNotes: Metallic-roughness PBR, metallic=0, roughness ~0.55-0.65 matte spheres with baked mottling/banding (no image textures). Pointer dots: small flat warm-amber discs stuck just proud of the surface. Axes: thin muted-grey line segments. Counters: dark text sprites. No emissive channels; the app handles any state highlight.
assetBrief: SUBJECT: A rotation row of five spheres along X: Mercury (-2.5, radius 0.24), Venus (-1.3, 0.4), Earth (0, 0.42), Mars (1.3, 0.3), Jupiter (2.6, 0.62). Each sphere spins about a shared visual Y-axis at its real relative rate, all locked to a master clock: Earth completes exactly one rotation per 24 virtual hours; Jupiter ~9.9h (fastest), Venus ~117 days (slowest, counterclockwise when viewed from above — opposite to the others), Mercury ~176 days, Mars 24.6h. A spin-up control multiplies the clock by up to 60× so slow spinners become observable; a day counter floats under each sphere (format HH:MM), pausing at each full day for learners who want to count. A small orange pointer-dot rides each surface so the rotation is visible. The retrograde indicator layer adds a half-arrow over Venus when enabled. The axis layer adds short dashed axis segments through each sphere center. Camera: full row framing [0, 1.2, 4.8] → target [0, 0.2, 0], planets evenly spaced, counters legible. Grounding: radial shadow beneath the row. Named groups per layers list.
